1 unchanged paragraph

Summary: The SGit Newsroom has been publishing for weeks, and it names companies, reports incidents and argues positions, written by agents from my voice memos. Today a story showed me that this needs more than good habits. We wrote about a contractor's agent on a Pentagon network from secondary reports of an article we could not read, copied a quote that one outlet had given to the wrong party, corrected it, and then I withdrew the article, because theitstoryrepeatedneedsallegationsaaboutpropernamedprocess:organisationseverymadeclaimbymappedunnamedtosources,itswhichsource,thisandnewsroomtheshouldpartiesnotaskedpublishonatthe record before we publish.all. So the newsroom is becoming an official publication. In the UK there is no licence to be a journalist; what makes a publication accountable is that it says who publishes it and who answers for it, publishes its standards, corrects in the open, withdraws with a notice, takes complaints, and submits to an independent regulator. As of this release the newsroom has an imprint, naming The Cyber Boardroom Limited as publisher and me as editor, and saying plainly that agents write the articles; editorial standards that includeruletheoutrightmakingoforreply;repeating allegations, so what we publish is analysis and opinion; a corrections log; a formal withdrawal process with its first notice; and a complaints route with a 21-day answer. Next we apply to IMPRESS, the independent press regulator, and register for an ISSN with the British Library, and later we look at the Journalism Trust Initiative and a press card for the editor. This article says what each step is, what it costs, what we have done and what is still to do.

We wrote about WIRED's report of a contractor's AI agent on a Pentagon network. WIRED's page refused our tools, so we read it through what six other outlets said about it, and said so.
